The Oregon recovery is measured against the freshly cut state in a harvest study, not against long-degraded land, and the paper does not say whether the regrowth was planted or natural [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. No unit comes from a low- or lower-middle-income setting. Expert positions point the other way: an FAO–CIFOR synthesis concludes that massive forestation programmes proclaimed as the answer to preventing floods simply will not do the job, although reforestation may bring other benefits [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_3], and a published comment argues that reforestation does not necessarily reduce flooding if soil properties do not recover, river bed morphology does not change and settlements, roads and drains remain unaltered [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_5]. Neither is a measurement; what separates them from the positive side is that they address flood prevention at large scale, while the review and the Oregon basin report peak flows in study catchments. No unit covers severe or extreme flood. For farmers the effect is off-site.
